q: Does BHT's cubic-root scaling hold empirically for r-to-one functions with r=4 or r=8, and does the small-N table-build regime dominate even more strongly, further depressing the fitted exponent?
basis: We tested only r=2 (the paper's primary case). Theorem 2 predicts O((N/r)^{1/3}) but the small-N deviation we saw for r=2 (fit slope 0.194 across all N, cleaning up to 0.314 only for N>=64) may worsen for larger r since k=(N/r)^{1/3} shrinks, making the classical table-build fraction of total queries even more constant-like.
next_steps: Extend make_two_to_one to make_r_to_one(N,r,seed); re-run the sweep with r in {2,4,8}; fit slopes on N>=64 and compare against 1/3; check if the r-dependent prefactor matches theory.

q: For the BHT claw-finding variant (two independent functions F, G), does the finite-size prefactor differ from collision-finding, and does the crossover with the classical baseline occur at a larger or smaller N?
basis: The paper extends the technique to claws but we only implemented collisions. Our collision replication showed a clear cross-over near N=64 where BHT starts outperforming birthday-attack; the claw variant has a different oracle structure (marking F(x)=G(y)) which could shift that cross-over.
next_steps: Implement Claw(F,G,k): pick k random y-values, hash G(y), Grover over x for F(x) in image(G-table). Sweep N and compare cross-over N against the collision case.

q: Under a depolarising or amplitude-damping noise model on the Grover oracle+diffusion, does the empirically optimal k shift upward relative to the ideal k=N^{1/3}, trading classical queries for reduced sensitivity to noisy quantum queries?
basis: Our clean statevector run saw Grover success probability ~0.95-1.0 per iteration. Under gate noise, the effective Grover success rate drops, requiring more retries or more Grover iterations per success — both of which would raise the effective per-query cost of the quantum step and rebalance the k tradeoff.
next_steps: Rerun the sweep on qiskit-aer's AerSimulator with 'depolarising' noise at 10^-3 per gate; for each N, sweep k around N^{1/3} and record wall-clock queries per success; compare optimal k vs the noiseless case.

q: For large k the classical lookup against table L costs O(log k) per Grover oracle call (or O(1) with hashing) — at what point does the invisible-to-the-query-metric wall-clock cost of maintaining and querying L overtake the F-evaluation cost, and does that shift the wall-clock-optimal k below N^{1/3}?
basis: The paper is explicit that they measure F-evaluations only, and briefly note that universal hashing can eliminate the O(sqrt(N) log N) sorting cost of the naive classical algorithm. Our replication also counts F-queries only; the actual wall-clock of the Grover oracle grows with |L|.
next_steps: Wall-clock benchmark each Grover iteration with L implemented as (a) sorted list + binary search, (b) hash set, (c) unrolled Boolean predicate compiled into the oracle unitary. Compare wall-clock optimal k vs query-optimal k for N up to 4096 or 8192.

q: Our reported query counts allow up to 8 retries of the Grover subroutine per BHT invocation. If we instead count expected queries per SUCCESSFUL run (single-shot Grover), does the log-log slope change materially, and does this exposure of the retry cost mask or amplify the quantum advantage?
basis: BHT theorem gives expected queries assuming standard amplitude amplification with O(1) expected retries — but the constant is not negligible at small N. Our success rate hit 100% for N>=16 partly because we allowed retries; the retry-inclusive metric could push the empirical slope up toward or past 1/3, or reveal a subtle metric-dependence.
next_steps: Modify bht_collision to record queries_including_failed_grover_attempts; refit the log-log slope on that metric; compare to the current 'successful-trial-queries' metric across the same N sweep.
